summary: Cloudflare follows up on the eMudhra CA weak intermediate key incident, describing how they patched internal systems (including AI-assisted code analysis to find trust points), logged handshakes in Pingora to detect forged certificates, and measured client patching via probe connections from challenge pages. It shows that modern browsers are mostly patched but bots, embedded WebViews, and many networks still accept the compromised chain, and argues for dynamically updatable trust stores.
title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys

summary: Explains a critical remote use-after-free in the Linux IPv4 TCP handshake: request-socket IP options were freed with kfree instead of kfree_rcu while other CPUs could still read them. Covers affected kernels and distro patch status, why Go's default MPTCP listeners matter, how to check hosts with ss -M, and an nftables mitigation that drops TCP packets carrying IPv4 options.
title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8

summary: Describes how Meta redesigned its Andromeda ads retrieval system by co-designing a mixture-of-experts retrieval model, fused GPU kernels, and a co-located single-GPU pipeline, reaching over a billion ads scored per second. It explains why retrieval at this scale is bound by memory bandwidth and network traffic, and how kernel fusion, moving index matching onto the GPU, and INT8 quantization address those limits.
title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design

summary: Rachel Laycock argues that experienced developers' hesitancy toward fully agentic coding stems from knowing that built software isn't the same as software that works in production. She describes a Thoughtworks experiment where a team built an app entirely with agents, spending most time on domain design and test/CI harnesses, yet struggled with a frequently red build, and she raises open questions about TDD, batch size, and CI/CD in the agentic era.
title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

summary: Podcast summary with Titus Winters covering Google's large-scale C++ refactoring (AST parsing via MapReduce, coexisting APIs, sharded changes), why Google mandated tests, and the readability review program. It also discusses AI's mixed effect on outages and productivity, plus critiques of the CS curriculum and career advice for new engineers.
title: Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters

summary: Meta describes PrivacyLib, a shared library embedded in clients of hundreds of data systems that enforces and observes privacy requirements at the point of data access via pluggable enforcing and observing modules. It covers how they achieve coverage (typed clients plus RPC boundaries), scale (build-time compiled policies, in-process caching for billions of checks/sec), and reliability (per-service rollout), with a concrete code walkthrough of Policy Zones protecting messaging metadata and agent-context propagation for AI agents.
title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary

summary: Meta describes its production system for LLM-generated 'catching' tests that run against risky diffs before landing. The system uses intent-aware and mutation-based 'dodgy diff' generation workflows, then filters false positives with an LLM-as-judge ensemble plus a rule-based assessor, escalating to engineers only when warranted. Reported results include a 60% true-positive rate and 74 serious privacy bugs caught at the diff stage.
title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale

summary: Martin Fowler argues that LLM-drafted prose carries a recognizable 'voice' that puts readers off, and advises writers not to let LLMs draft or rephrase their work, though outlines may be acceptable. He frames writing as a tool for thinking, so delegating it to LLMs means delegating comprehension too. He also covers exceptions such as disability, translation, and form documents, and describes his site's AI-disclosure policy.
title: LLM Voice

summary: Netflix describes how Pensive, its system for auto-diagnosing and remediating failed data workloads across Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid, moved from regex and hand-written Java rules to an AI-assisted approach. The piece covers the scale involved (around 100k failures on peak days), how errors are classified into user versus platform causes, and how the system produces retry or remediation guidance reliably.
title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

summary: Netflix describes an automated system that reframes horizontal video into vertical and other aspect ratios for its in-app Clips feed and social marketing, replacing manual editor reframing. The post covers how cropping decisions are made and how the system plugs into internal production tooling at scale.
title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing

summary: Cloudflare explains how Privacy Pass and its successor MOLE (issuer-hiding endorsements and credentials) can move to post-quantum cryptography. It covers why token privacy already survives quantum attacks while unforgeability does not, and introduces VOLE-in-the-Head zero-knowledge proofs, MQ-based signatures like KuMQuat and UOV, and the tradeoffs in signature size and composability.
title: The post-quantum future of web privacy

summary: Dropbox describes the architecture behind its file-acting AI agent. The agent runs in per-conversation QEMU snapshot-restored VMs that come up in milliseconds and reach Dropbox files through rclone. Permission checks and credential injection sit in a host-side proxy outside the VM, and the piece also covers the Codex App Server JSON-RPC protocol (threads/turns/items), harness adapters, plan approval, and version-history rollback.
title: How two engineer side projects became the agent taking action inside Dropbox

summary: Describes building a Virtio-FS driver for Redox OS and porting it to boot on Cloud Hypervisor, including an explanation of how hardware virtualization, nested paging, and VirtIO devices work. Walks through concrete bugs encountered, such as legacy 8259 interrupt routing and a missing PIT/HPET timer that broke sleeps and preemption, fixed by using the local APIC TSC-deadline timer.
title: Virtualized Redox: from Virtio-FS to Cloud Hypervisor, and beyond

summary: Explains read, write, and space amplification as the gap between logical database requests and the physical storage work they trigger. Compares how B-trees and LSM trees trade off these amplifications, and covers how indexes, Bloom filters, compression, and caching affect them. The provided text is only the introduction and outline, so how deep the full article goes is unclear.
title: The Hidden Work Behind Every Database Request

summary: Podcast episode notes with Maude Lemaire covering scaling challenges at Slack and GitHub: thundering herds from emoji reactions in huge channels, event floods for power users, building the Koi Pond load-testing tool for 500k WebSocket connections, and how ActiveRecord-driven scatter queries capped GitHub at 16 shards. It also touches on using AI for foundational work and rotating platform and product engineers.
title: Scaling Slack and GitHub with Maude Lemaire

summary: Applies the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model to self-service platforms for data mesh and data products, using domain storytelling to contrast provisional, operational, scalable, and optimizing levels. It explains the 'platform gap' between data product/contract concepts and underlying tools like Spark, Iceberg, and S3, and why ticketing and IaC scripts alone still leave developers gluing components together.
title: The Data Product Platform Navigator

summary: Meta describes F3 Lightning, which decouples per-feature releases of ads ML features from a single merged compute graph while keeping shared execution efficiency. It covers content-derived stable identifiers for deduplicating computation, building a single flattened execution plan at startup with failure isolation, a shared per-request memory buffer for cache locality, and dense index mapping to remove hash lookups. The result is ~3.6x faster time-to-production with no added compute cost.
title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale

summary: Cloudflare argues that remotely hosted AI agents act as intermediaries that strip websites of the identity, reputation, and accountability signals they use for fraud prevention, monetization, and compliance. It catalogs concrete problems such as friendly fraud, traffic commingling, broken risk-based auth, and account sharing. It also explains why human-in-the-loop CAPTCHAs and scoped permissions fail to solve them, and proposes the principle that the user–site relationship must survive intermediation.
title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)

summary: Pinterest engineers describe how they pre-train large ID embedding tables and fine-tune them inside the Homefeed ranking model. The focus is on making multi-epoch training safe, meaning it avoids the overfitting that is typical when ID embeddings see the same data repeatedly, while keeping the infrastructure efficient. The excerpt is truncated, so how deep the detail goes is uncertain.
title: Safe and Efficient Multi-Epoch Embedding Training

summary: Presents AutoParallel, a PyTorch-native planner that jointly searches parallelization strategies (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) for distributed training and emits ordinary PyTorch programs that compose with the compile stack and user-written distributed code. On dense, hybrid and MoE models across up to 128 H100s, it matches or beats expert TorchTitan recipes by up to 18.3% throughput and finds plans that hand-written recipes don't express.
title: AutoParallel: Composable, PyTorch-Native Automatic Parallelism for Production Training
